item.title: Exponentially Compressed and Garbage-Free Alias Sampling for Polynomial State Preparation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructs an exponentially compressed, deterministic, garbage-free Clifford+T circuit preparing polynomial states of degree d on n qubits with total gate count O~(ndB+B(B+log⁡(1/ϵ))log⁡(B/ϵ)), using an ordered alias table represented in O(d(n+B)) bits.

Grade 0.450 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Diyi Liu, Hanyu Wang, Shuchen Zhu, Jason Cong, Wibe Albert de Jong, David Williams-Young, Chao Yang

Figure

End-to-end workflow showing classical extraction of group and finite-difference parameters followed by coherent superposition preparation, implicit alias table evaluation, and inverse fiber ranking to uncompute ancillae.

Asks

Can a alias sampling based method prepare a polynomial state on a 2n-point grid at poly⁡(n) cost while leaving no auxiliary register entangled with the output?

Before

Standard alias table construction and storage required Θ(2n) classical and quantum cost.

But

Real polynomial amplitudes of degree at most d, integer grid points N=2n, and bit width B=O(β+dn+dlog⁡(d+1)) for coefficient bit length β.

Tools

coherent alias sampling · fiber ranking uncomputation · reversible integer arithmetic · Newton-Raphson iteration · finite-difference cumulative summation

Abstract

Coherent alias sampling implement an important subroutine for block encoding and qubitization based quantum simulation using quantum lookup table. Related constructions exploit data lookup and matrix structure to implement block encodings for use in quantum singular value transformation. For a state on n qubits, constructing and storing the alias table requires both classical and quantum resources exponential in n. We show that when the amplitudes are samples of a polynomial of degree at most d, the table can be represented and evaluated coherently with cost polynomial in n, d, exponentially reduced from Θ(2ⁿ) classical and quantum cost. We construct a quantum circuit for coherently computing the alias table for polynomial states using reversible integer arithmetic. By employing fast arithmetic, we construct a deterministic circuit for preparing polynomial states over Clifford+T with a complete gate count of tildeO(ndB+B²), where arithmetic width B=tildeO(dn+dlog(d+1)). In the high precision limit for state fidelity ε with fixed n and d, it is sufficient have B=Θ(log(1/ε)) and the complete gate count becomes O(log³(1/ε)loglog(1/ε)). Additionally, the effective representation of the alias table can also be used for classical sampling algorithms. Furthermore, we develop a novel technique for uncomputing the auxilary register generated by coherent alias sampling. This technique opens a research direction in sampling based initial state preparation.

item.title: Random-Oracle Unitary Synthesis is Impossible
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Random-oracle unitary synthesis requires k≥N/poly⁡(n) queries to the random oracle for dimension N=2n. In the ROM-PRU model, no Ω(N1+γ) unitary design on n qubits is efficiently achievable for any γ>0, while an O(N)-design is constructed with poly⁡(n) queries.

Grade 0.439 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Andrew Huang, Akshar Ramkumar, John Wright

Asks

Can an arbitrary or Haar-random unitary be synthesized efficiently on a quantum computer given access to a random Boolean oracle?

Before

Best previous ROM pseudorandom unitary constructions achieved o(N)-query security (Ma and Huang 2024), while synthesis single-query lower bounds (Fefferman and Lin 2024) and two-query extensions (Chen et al. 2024) did not rule out polynomial-query synthesis.

But

Lower bound holds for diamond-norm error ϵ≤1−1/poly⁡(n). The O(N)-query PRU construction uses poly⁡(n) oracle queries but is not shown to be computationally efficient in gate count.

Tools

representation theory of unitary groups · Schur's lemma · Robinson-Schensted-Knuth correspondence · diamond norm error bounds

Abstract

A major open problem in quantum complexity is the question of unitary synthesis---namely, is it possible to efficiently implement any unitary, given the ability to evaluate any classical function in superposition? Inspired by a recent work by Brakerski and Yuen (CRYPTO 2026), we propose an ``average-case'' unitary synthesis problem, which asks whether it is possible to efficiently implement a Haar random unitary given access to a random Boolean function. We then demonstrate a superpolynomial query lower bound, establishing that unitary synthesis in this model is impossible. Along with our main result, we settle in the negative a question Brakerski and Yuen pose, of whether scalable pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) can be implemented in the ROM-PRU model. In particular, we show that in the ROM-PRU model, no Ω(N^(1+γ)) unitary design on n qubits, where N=2ⁿ, can be efficiently achieved for any γ> 0. On the other hand, we construct an O(N)-design in poly(n) queries in the same model, surpassing the previously best known results which constructed O(√N)-designs.

item.title: Robustness of Quantum Signal Processing and Resource-aware Polynomial Design
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Linear-in-error robustness bounds for quantum signal processing based on the operator-Lipschitz constant L⋆ reduce fault-tolerant T-gate counts by 51.9%--56.7% compared to error-function polynomials.

Grade 0.426 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Thiago O. Maciel, Giancarlo Camilo, Allan Tosta, Daniel Stilck-Francca, Leandro Aolita, Thais de Lima Silva

Figure

Modeled resource advantage (T-gate reduction) and operator-Lipschitz robustness advantage across multiple fixed-hardware profiles (εfp,εsynth) at fixed total error ε=0.010 for the H6 Hamiltonian.

Asks

How do operator-encoding perturbations and discrete gate-synthesis errors propagate through quantum signal processing circuits to affect overall fault-tolerant resource requirements?

Before

Analytical error-function approximation polynomials with QSVT robustness bounds that scale with logarithmic or square-root factors of input error.

But

Tested specifically on eigenvalue thresholding for the H6 molecular Hamiltonian under an LCU input access model; polynomial-design optimization guarantees local rather than global cost minimality.

Tools

Operator-Lipschitz continuity · Finite-dimensional active-set exchange algorithm · Linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · Remez-type linear program

Abstract

Quantum signal processing (QSP) realizes operator functions through polynomial transformations of a finite degree. In addition to function approximation errors, realistic implementations incur algorithmic errors also when encoding the input operator and in synthesizing gates into a discrete fault-tolerant gate set. We provide an end-to-end analysis of these errors and show that the input error propagation is governed by the operator-Lipschitz constant L_⋆ of the implemented function. We then derive an efficient classical algorithm to compute tight lower and upper bounds on L_⋆, and we show that these bounds induce in turn lower and upper bounds on the total quantum-resource cost (for instance, T-gate count) needed for QSP implementations compatible with a target total error. We further devise a procedure to search for a polynomial with minimum cost based solely on its coefficients, yielding a resource-aware polynomial-design procedure for QSP. We illustrate the resulting method for ground state energy estimation via eigenvalue thresholding for the H₆ molecular Hamiltonian. In the tested hardware profiles, the resource-aware family improves the total-error budget and reduces the modeled T-gate count by 51.9%--56.7% relative to the standard analytical polynomial obtained from an error-function approximation.

item.title: Training Variational Quantum Algorithms Is NP-Hard, Even Locally
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Finding a local minimizer of a variational quantum algorithm training objective, or finding any parameter vector within ℓp-distance strictly less than π/2 of one for all p≥1, is strongly 𝖭𝖯-hard.

Grade 0.425 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Dax Enshan Koh, Triscia Mundo, Iosif Sakos, Antonios Varvitsiotis

Figure

Parameter domains Θ=[0,2π]2 and transformed coordinate space 𝒳=[0,1]2. The plot illustrates the separation between local minimizers at corner coordinates versus boundary regions depending on whether the graph stability number α(G)<k or α(G)≥k.

Asks

Can the computational barrier to variational quantum algorithm training be avoided if the goal is only to find a local minimizer or a point close to one?

Before

Global minimization of variational quantum algorithm training objectives was known to be 𝖭𝖯-hard (Bittel and Kliesch 2021).

But

Worst-case computational complexity setting. Holds even for circuits using only 2n single-qubit gates, 2n qubits, and efficiently evaluable diagonal two-local observables.

Tools

polynomial-time reduction from Stable Set · Hermitian trigonometric polynomials · parameterized quantum circuits with single-qubit rotations · commuting diagonal two-local observables

Abstract

Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) generally rely on classical optimization to train parameterized quantum circuits. This training seeks to minimize an objective function, and its efficiency is central to the practical success of these algorithms. However, globally minimizing such training objectives over the circuit parameters is known to be NP-hard, limiting the prospect of general guarantees for efficient training. In this Letter, we prove that even the weaker task of finding a local minimum of such VQA training objectives is strongly NP-hard, including when the objective admits efficient classical evaluation. Moreover, we show that this hardness persists even for the task of finding a parameter vector within ℓ_p-distance strictly less than π/2 of some local minimizer, for every p≥1. Our central technical result is that approximating a local minimizer of a Hermitian trigonometric polynomial is strongly NP-hard. By explicitly constructing quantum circuits whose training objectives reproduce these hard instances, we obtain a polynomial-time reduction to VQA training. Our results establish a fundamental computational barrier to variational quantum training: even reaching the vicinity of a local minimum remains hard in the worst case.

item.title: Parallelizing Dissipative Quantum Algorithms
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Parallel bulk dissipation reduces total query depth asymptotically from 𝒪~(n5) to 𝒪~(n) on a 1D transverse-field Ising chain, yielding a 53x query depth reduction for n=100 qubits at relative energy error 10−3.

Grade 0.421 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Sudatta Hor, Nathan Wiebe, Yongshan Ding

Figure

System energy Et versus theoretical upper bound on query depth for single, boundary, sequential bulk, and parallel bulk dissipation (r=4,10,16) on a 100-qubit 1D TFIM.

Asks

How can the high circuit depth caused by sequential bulk dissipation jump operators be reduced in dissipative quantum state preparation algorithms?

Before

Sequential bulk dissipation required total depth 𝒪~(n5) (Kashani et al. 2024), while single-jump dissipation required 𝒪~(n9) (Ding et al. 2024).

But

Applies to Hamiltonians with geometric locality and filter functions with rapidly decaying tails |f(t)|≤Ce−μ|t|. Numerical results evaluated on 1D spin chain without hardware noise.

Tools

Lieb-Robinson bounds · First-order Trotter Lindbladian simulation · Stinespring dilation · Quasi-free fermionic Lindblad dynamics simulation

Abstract

Inspired by classical Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, dissipative quantum algorithms are an emerging class of methods for preparing quantum states on a quantum computer. They operate by simulating a dissipative process governed by a mathematical operator known as the Lindbladian. The performance of these algorithms can be limited by the sequential implementation of the Lindbladian's constituent jump operators, which leads to high circuit depth. To address this issue, this work analyzes a parallelization scheme to implement jump operators simultaneously. We leverage the structure of geometric locality to show that individual jump operators remain spatially localized. This exponentially reduces the circuit depth per time step, resulting in an overall polynomial improvement. Numerical experiments demonstrate a 53x reduction in query depth for a 1D benchmark system of 100 qubits. The reduced circuit depth makes dissipative algorithms more practical for near-term quantum computing.

item.title: An efficient Hamiltonian-based quantum algorithm for characters of the symmetric group
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Character state preparation (CSP) over Sn implemented by sequenced Hamiltonian evolutions in provably O~(n2.5) gates in worst case, extending to a general quantum character transform (QCT) in O~(n2.5) gates using O(n) qubits.

Grade 0.420 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Dikshant Rathore, Leo Zhou

Figure

Total Trotter steps Mtot required to achieve final-state error 10−2 as a function of n (8≤n≤30) across uniform cycle types (sm) and candidate quantum-advantage partitions, fitted against power laws.

Asks

Can quantum states encoding arbitrary columns and the full character transform of the symmetric group Sn be prepared more simply and with lower gate complexity than using the quantum Fourier transform?

Before

Best previous CSP used the Sn quantum Fourier transform requiring O~(n3) gates and O~(n3/2) qubits (Bravyi et al. 2025).

But

Worst-case O~(n2.5) gate complexity bound requires QSVT; Trotter bounds for uniform cycle types (sm) rely on leading-order state-dependent analysis without proven bounds on higher-order remainders.

Tools

Hamiltonian simulation · Jordan-Wigner fermionic current operators · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · State-dependent Trotter error bounds · Reconfigurable qubit architectures

Abstract

Consider a quantum state vector proportional to any given column of the character table of the symmetric group (S_n), corresponding to a superposition over the irreps weighted by the character values. It was recently argued that sampling from this state is classically hard under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, while there exists an efficient quantum algorithm for preparing this character state using the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) over S_n [arXiv:2501.12579]. We give an alternative, simpler algorithm to prepare this character state with a sequence of Hamiltonian evolutions, as well as an efficient implementation with reconfigurable qubits that uses only nearest-neighbor gates in 1D. The gate complexity, accounting for Hamiltonian simulation errors, depends on the choice of the column: For fixed target state error, the estimated sufficient total gate count ranges from as few as O(n) gates for the n-cycle column, to widetildeO(n^(1.75)) gates near the conjecturally classically hard parameter regime, to provably widetildeO(n^(2.5)) gates in the worst case. In contrast, the QFT subroutine in the prior approach uses widetildeO(n³) gates. Our gate count estimates come from leading-order state-dependent Trotter error analysis, and the proven worst-case bound relies on a QSVT-based Hamiltonian simulation method; numerical benchmarks of the Trotter-based protocol suggest that the estimates are conservative. Furthermore, we generalize our protocol to give an explicit algorithm for the quantum character transform (QCT) over S_n using widetildeO(n^(2.5)) gates and O(n) qubits. An application to entanglement entropy of symmetric orbifold conformal field theories is also discussed.

item.arxave:abstract: Consider a quantum state vector proportional to any given column of the character table of the symmetric group (S_n), corresponding to a superposition over the irreps weighted by the character values. It was recently argued that sampling from this state is classically hard under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, while there exists an efficient quantum algorithm for preparing this character state using the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) over S_n [arXiv:2501.12579]. We give an alternative, simpler algorithm to prepare this character state with a sequence of Hamiltonian evolutions, as well as an efficient implementation with reconfigurable qubits that uses only nearest-neighbor gates in 1D. The gate complexity, accounting for Hamiltonian simulation errors, depends on the choice of the column: For fixed target state error, the estimated sufficient total gate count ranges from as few as O(n) gates for the n-cycle column, to widetildeO(n^(1.75)) gates near the conjecturally classically hard parameter regime, to provably widetildeO(n^(2.5)) gates in the worst case. In contrast, the QFT subroutine in the prior approach uses widetildeO(n³) gates. Our gate count estimates come from leading-order state-dependent Trotter error analysis, and the proven worst-case bound relies on a QSVT-based Hamiltonian simulation method; numerical benchmarks of the Trotter-based protocol suggest that the estimates are conservative. Furthermore, we generalize our protocol to give an explicit algorithm for the quantum character transform (QCT) over S_n using widetildeO(n^(2.5)) gates and O(n) qubits. An application to entanglement entropy of symmetric orbifold conformal field theories is also discussed.
